title: Facial Emotion Recognition in Gifted Children: An Early Phase Advantage?
abstract: The literature suggests that gifted children outperform peers in information-processing tasks. Also, research shows that facial emotion recognition accuracy is affected by expression intensity, which can be depicted as different amounts of information available for the observer during the emotion recognition process. To test if an information-processing advantage for gifted children also exists in the emotional domain, in this study we compared gifted children’s and a control peer group’s performance on dynamic facial emotion recognition as expressed at different intensity levels (40–100%). Participants (7–11 years old) completed an emotional recognition task involving six basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise) presented as morphed videoclips. A strong positive correlation between age and general accuracy was found within the whole sample, confirming that the ability develops progressively as children mature. Results indicated that the gifted group shows significantly higher accuracy on disgust and surprise recognition. An interaction effect group by intensity level was found, with the gifted group reporting significantly better performance in accuracy at low intensity (40%) compared to controls, indicating that their advantage in information-processing may be more detectable in the early phase of emotion expression, despite the emotion’s type. Future studies are needed to clarify the nature of these results.
